lines.text: November, twenty thirteen.
An inventor walks onto the set of Shark Tank, carrying a doorbell.
He asks for seven hundred thousand dollars, for ten percent of his company.
Four Sharks say no. The fifth makes an offer he won't accept.
He walks away with nothing.
Five years later, Amazon would buy that company, in a deal reported to be worth more than a billion dollars.
This is the story of the billion dollar no.
Twenty eleven. Jamie Siminoff is a tinkerer, building gadgets in his garage in Southern California.
And he has a problem. When someone rings the front door, he can't hear it from the garage.
So he does what inventors do. He connects the doorbell to Wi-Fi, adds a camera, and sends the front door to his phone.
He calls it DoorBot.
A camera.
A button.
A radio.
Answer the door, from anywhere.
The early hardware is rough, and money is tight.
So he takes the biggest swing he can find. National television.
In the Tank, Siminoff values DoorBot at seven million dollars. It sells for about two hundred.
One by one, the Sharks find their reasons.
Lori Greiner doesn't see enough to set it apart at that price.
Daymond John worries the big security companies could crush it.
Robert Herjavec questions whether a connected device could be hacked.
Mark Cuban can't see the path to a company worth tens of millions.
Only Kevin O'Leary makes an offer. Seven hundred thousand, structured like a loan, repaid through royalties on every unit sold, plus a slice of equity.
For a young hardware company, terms like that can be suffocating. Siminoff says no.
No deal.
On paper, it's a failure. But when the episode airs, millions of viewers have just met DoorBot. And the orders start coming in.
The rejection doesn't end the company. It sharpens it.
Siminoff rebuilds the product, piece by piece. Better video. Better design. A bigger mission.
And in September twenty fourteen, DoorBot gets a new name.
Ring.
Not just a doorbell, but a promise: to make neighborhoods safer.
Then, an email arrives. From Richard Branson.
In twenty fifteen, Branson helps lead a twenty eight million dollar round.
In twenty sixteen, Kleiner Perkins leads sixty one million more.
In twenty seventeen, one hundred and nine million, with backers including DFJ Growth, Goldman Sachs, and Qualcomm Ventures.
In all, more than two hundred million dollars of venture funding, for the company the Sharks passed on.
Ring isn't a gadget anymore. It's a system.
Video doorbells.
Floodlight cameras.
Stick up cams.
A home alarm.
Front door by front door, porch lights turn blue, all across the map.
And the value of the company climbs.
Seven million, asked for in the Tank.
About sixty million, in twenty fifteen.
Two hundred and four million, in twenty sixteen.
Four hundred and forty five million, in twenty seventeen.
The doorbell that couldn't find an investor on television, now has some of the biggest names in finance behind it.
And the biggest name in e-commerce is paying attention.
February twenty seventh, twenty eighteen.
Amazon announces it will acquire Ring.
The terms aren't disclosed. But reports put the price at more than one billion dollars.
From a seven hundred thousand dollar ask, to a billion dollar exit.
That October, Jamie Siminoff returns to Shark Tank. This time, he's sitting in the Shark's chair.
Sometimes, the most important deal you'll ever make...
is the one you walk away from.
